aspects.says: A method receives a copy of the caller's reference: it can change the caller's object but not the caller's variable.
basis: section:Assignment Copies the Reference, Not the Object
aspects.reason: one sentence here; passing arguments is the subject of unit 1.3.3, which carries its own practice

aspects.says: Assigning a reference copies the reference, so two variables reach one object and a change through either is seen through both.
basis: section:Assignment Copies the Reference, Not the Object

aspects.says: Objects.requireNonNull where a reference enters an object moves the NullPointerException from where the null is used to where it was passed.
basis: section:A Reference Field or Array Element Starts as null, and the NPE Comes Where It Is Used
aspects.reason: the difference is which stack frame throws; a test of the reader's method sees the same exception type either way

aspects.says: An independent copy copies every mutable level, nested collections included, or makes the lower levels immutable.
basis: section:A Copy Is Only as Deep as the Code That Made It

aspects.says: List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list of the same elements: it can't be added to, and its elements can still be changed.
basis: section:A Copy Is Only as Deep as the Code That Made It

aspects.says: == on references is true only for one object: string literals and compile-time constants share one object, while strings built at run time are new objects, so equals compares the text.
basis: section:== Compares References; equals Compares What the Class Defines

aspects.says: A local variable has no default value; reading it before assignment is a compile error.
basis: section:A Reference Field or Array Element Starts as null, and the NPE Comes Where It Is Used
aspects.reason: a compile-time rule: no wrong solution compiles, so no test can grade it

aspects.says: A reference that may be missing has to be checked before a method is called on it; equals on a null receiver throws.
basis: section:A Reference Field or Array Element Starts as null, and the NPE Comes Where It Is Used

aspects.says: A class that doesn't override equals inherits Object.equals, which compares identity, so a set never finds an equal-looking new object; a record's equals compares components.
basis: section:== Compares References; equals Compares What the Class Defines
aspects.reason: writing equals and hashCode belongs to the record and class units (2.4.1); this page only shows the default, which a practice could check only by having the reader write equals

aspects.says: The collector keeps what it can reach from the GC roots; an unreachable cycle is collected, and anything a static field reaches is kept.
basis: section:An Object Lives While Something Reachable Refers to It

aspects.says: Reference fields and array elements start as null, and new T[n] creates no T objects.
basis: section:A Reference Field or Array Element Starts as null, and the NPE Comes Where It Is Used

aspects.says: A copy made with new ArrayList<>(list) is a new list of the same element objects, so a change to an element reaches the original.
basis: section:A Copy Is Only as Deep as the Code That Made It

aspects.says: A static collection that only grows keeps every entry reachable, so the heap after collection grows until OutOfMemoryError.
basis: section:An Object Lives While Something Reachable Refers to It

aspects.says: System.gc() is a request; the JVM collects on its own, and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns the request off.
basis: section:An Object Lives While Something Reachable Refers to It
